data.title: The Evolution of Team Performance in Professional League of Legends
data.research_question: How persistent is team strength from split to split, how has the spread of team performance changed across seasons, and which teams were consistently strong?
data.motivation: Persistence measures how durable competitive advantages are. Strong persistence suggests stable organisations and rosters; weak persistence suggests results driven by short-term factors or roster turnover. The seasonal spread shows whether the field became more or less even.
methodology: Persistence: regular-season win% of the same team id in consecutive splits of the same league; Pearson and Spearman correlation and OLS slope.
Seasonal spread: per calendar year, quantiles (10th to 90th) of win% across teams with 20+ games.
Consistency: mean and standard deviation of split win% for teams with 6+ splits.
Elo trajectories: rating after each game (Elo with league offsets).
limitations: A team id can carry a very different roster across splits.
Teams that are relegated or leave a league drop out (survivorship).
Win% has sampling noise, which biases the persistence slope toward zero (attenuation).
Calendar years differ in league coverage in the source, so trend lines mix changes in competition with changes in coverage.
references: Fort, R., & Quirk, J. (1995). Cross-subsidization, incentives, and outcomes in professional team sports leagues. Journal of Economic Literature, 33(3), 1265-1299.
Elo, A. E. (1978). The Rating of Chessplayers, Past and Present. Arco Publishing.
Sevenhuysen, T. Oracle's Elixir: LoL esports match data. https://oracleselixir.com/tools/downloads

data.source: Oracle's Elixir professional League of Legends match data (yearly CSV files).

persistence.definition: Regular-season win % of the same team (same team id) in consecutive splits of the same league. Pearson and Spearman correlation and OLS slope of win% t+1 on win% t. A slope below 1 indicates regression toward 0.5.

season_trends.definition: Calendar years. Active team = at least one game in the year. Win % quantiles across teams with 20+ games that year (a wide spread = unequal results).

team_consistency.definition: Teams with at least 6 regular-season splits of 5+ games. Mean and standard deviation of split win %. A low standard deviation at a high mean = consistently strong.

findings: Correlation of win% between splits: Pearson 0.42, Spearman 0.42; OLS slope 0.42.
Spread of team win% (90th minus 10th percentile, teams with 20+ games): 0.404 in 2020 and 0.354 in 2026 (7 years with 50+ such teams).
Highest mean split win% among teams with 8+ splits: PSG Talon (PCS), 77.3% over 14 splits (sd 0.165).
data.interpretation: A slope of 0.42 means a team 10 points above .500 in one split is expected to be about 4.2 points above .500 in the next: partial regression toward the middle. Part of this regression is measurement noise from short splits, so true persistence is somewhat higher than the slope suggests.
